title: LEXICANUM VAULT — STACK THETA, EFFECTS HOLDING
intro:
Stack Theta is four degrees colder than Delta and has no shelving in it at
all. It is a floor, a wire CAGE the size of a chapel, and the effects of
everybody who has died in the Adamant Crown's service since 934 and not been
claimed by a family.

Under-Clerk Habrach meets you at the gate with a slate and no enthusiasm, and
reads the requisition twice, and finds it entirely in order, which visibly
disappoints him.

"Vosk, H. Nine — sorry. Seven crates."

He unlocks the outer gate. Inside the cage, stencilled in somebody's careful
hand on plain grey board, with his name on every one of them:

Nine crates.
revisit: Four degrees, a wire cage the size of a chapel, and nine crates with a dead man's name stencilled on them.
look:
A wire CAGE, a concrete floor, and no shelving. Everything in Stack Theta is
in a box and none of the boxes are interesting to anybody.

Nine CRATES, stencilled VOSK H. The MANIFEST on Habrach's slate, which says
seven.

Under-Clerk HABRACH, waiting to be finished with.

objects.careless: Effects manifest, VOSK H., raised at the close of the case by the Provost's office and countersigned by the Lexicanum on receipt. Seven crates.
objects.careful:
You read it properly, which takes four minutes, because a manifest is a boring document and boring documents are read by nobody.

Seven crates. Contents by crate, itemised, in the flat vocabulary of a stock return.

Crate three: *gaming set, incomplete.*

He had a regicide board with three illegal pieces on it, arranged into a Vault shelf-address, and the return calls it a gaming set and calls it incomplete, and *incomplete* is not a word a stock clerk uses about a board with all its pieces on it.

There is no line for footwear.

Not *footwear, one pair, unremarkable*. Not a line at all. Two crates and a pair of boots have been taken off a stock return for a dead Inquisitor's effects, and the return was countersigned on receipt by a Lexicanum clerk who counted what was in front of him.

objects.careless: Nine crates, plain grey board, VOSK H. stencilled on each of them in the same careful hand.
objects.careful:
Seven crates, says the manifest.

You count nine.

You count them again, because the number is not interesting enough to be wrong. Nine crates, seven listed, and the two that do not exist are sitting in the cage in front of you with his name stencilled on them in somebody's careful hand.

Whatever has been editing this hive can reach the paper.

It cannot reach the boots.

You stand in the cold of Stack Theta for a while, holding that, turning it over, and find it a very great deal more frightening than the alternative.

objects.careless: A wire cage the size of a chapel, with an inner gate that is locked and a padlock the size of a fist.
objects.careful:
The inner gate takes a countersign, which is ordinary: effects are property, property has a claimant, and the Crown does not let an officer open a dead colleague's crates on his own signature.

The countersigning seat for Ordo effects on this world is the Administratum's Vardan reconciliation office.

It is signed A. KESH, and it is signed in advance, on a standing instrument, for anything of Vosk's that anybody ever asks for.

Habrach has no idea why you have gone quiet.

objects.careless: The regicide board, folded, and the pieces loose in a cloth bag beside it, because whoever packed it did what anybody would do with a board and some pieces.
objects.careful:
The positions are gone. They were gone eight days after he died, when two Provost men who had never played regicide in their lives folded the board and put the pieces in a bag.

So you do it the long way, with the Provost's own pict-captures out of your case-file on the floor beside you and the pieces in your hand, one at a time, for most of an afternoon.

Three of them are on squares no legal game reaches.

D2. F4. C9. A Vault shelf-address in furniture, four days late and four degrees cold, and it is the same address it was on the morning he died.

objects.careless: The Provost's scene captures, eleven of them, pulled out of your own case-file. Standard procedure, taken before anything was moved.
objects.careful:
The window is in four of the eleven, because the Provost's man stood where you would have stood.

The west shutter is not shut and is not open. It is at four degrees, which is a setting nobody has ever chosen for a shutter, and it is at four degrees in all four captures.

Four degrees is the twelfth hour, and the twelfth hour is cell four, and cell four is a number he could not write down.

It has been in your case-file since the fourth hour of the first morning and it was in front of you the whole time and you were looking at the body.

objects.careless: The auto-quill and its blotter, packed together, and a brass censer wrapped in cloth by somebody who thought it was a censer.
objects.careful:
The blotter took the reverse of everything the quill wrote for the last four days of his life, and the Provost's men packed it flat and face-down and it has not been touched since.

Nine hundred glyphs and more, in a hand that runs right to left, written in one sitting and burned four minutes later.

The quill's own counter agrees: one entry, that length, at the twenty-third hour and fifty-one.

He wrote it, and he burned it, and then he sat down at the board.

objects.careless: The desk pad, curled at one corner from eight days in a crate, with a year of a dead man's appointments on it.
objects.careful:
Six days circled twice, in the last fortnight, and nothing written against any of them.

You go back through the pad and then through the four before it, which are in the same crate, because he kept them.

The circles go back eighty-one years at eighty-four-day intervals and they are in four different inks and one of them is not his hand.

There is no entry against a single one of them. In eighty-one years of a man who wrote everything down, six days a year have nothing at all written against them, and there is no record anywhere in this hive of what any of them were for.

objects.take_text:
You take them.

There is no line on the manifest to strike and no crate to sign out and no clerk who will ever be asked about it, because as far as the Lexicanum Vault is concerned you have removed nothing from Stack Theta at all.

You carry a dead man's boots out of the Adamant Crown under your coat like a thief, and it is the safest thing you have done in eleven weeks.

[ VOSK_BOOTS ]
objects.careful:
They are the wrong boots.

Not worn wrong, not laced wrong — *the wrong boots*, his left on the right and his right on the left, and a man does not do that to himself at the end of a long night by accident.

Sarrow's Reach. A rest-halt, a corporal with sixteen years, and a way of telling the man behind you to read the ground backwards without saying anything a listener could report.

You learned it when you were twenty-six and too frightened to eat.

He is not on the manifest. He was never on the manifest. Whatever went through this record and took two crates out of a stock return went past a pair of boots on a mortuary shelf and could not see them, because there has never been a form in the Imperium with a field for what a man's feet are saying.

npcs.title: Under-Clerk Habrach
npcs.topic_refusal: "Ask," Habrach says. "I'll tell you if it's on the slate."
npcs.portrait: Under-Clerk Habrach, in a coat and fingerless gloves, holding a slate and waiting to be finished with. Stack Theta is the coldest posting in the Vault and he has had it for nine years.
npcs.greeting:
"Vosk, H.," Habrach says. "Effects holding, closed matter, reopened. It's all in order and I've read it twice and I'd rather you were quick, because the heaters in Theta went in 'ninety-one and nobody's raised a docket."

He does not ask what you want with them. Nobody in this building has asked you anything for a fortnight.
npcs.reprise: He waits by the gate with the slate, entirely unbothered, extremely cold.
deflect: "Anything else," he says, in the voice of a man who does not mean it as a question.

topics.text:
"Seven," Habrach says, from the slate, without looking up.

"There are nine."

He looks up. He goes into the cage and counts them, touching each one, the way a man counts when he already knows the answer and is being made to prove it.

"Nine," he agrees.

He stands there for a moment with his hand on the ninth crate.

"That's a receipting error, that is. I'll raise it." He is already writing. "Nine in, seven on the return, countersigned by me on the day, which means either I counted seven crates that were nine or somebody's had two out and put them back."

"Which do you think it is?"

"I counted nine, sir." Flatly. "I count things. It's the job. I've been doing it nine years in a room with no heating and the one thing I do not get wrong is a number in front of my face."

He finishes writing and looks at what he has written and does not raise it.

"I'll leave that," he says, after a while, and rubs it out with his thumb.

"Didn't know him. Saw him four times."

Habrach considers whether that is the end of the answer and decides it is not.

"He came down here himself, which they don't. Twice about a clerk's effects — Ordinate's widow, nothing in it, no claim — and once about a man off the Choir whose family couldn't be found, and he sat on a crate in this cold for an hour reading what was in it so that he could write to somebody who might have known him."

"And the fourth?"

"Fourth was eleven weeks ago and he asked me how the manifests are amended." Habrach shrugs. "Told him: they aren't. You raise a new one. He said *thank you*, like I'd given him something, and went away up the stairs."

"They aren't amended," Habrach says. "That's the whole point of them. A manifest is what was counted on the day by the man who counted it, and if the count's wrong you raise a *new* one, and the old one stays, because otherwise what have you got."

"And if the old one changed anyway."

"Then it isn't a manifest. It's just a piece of paper with numbers on it."

He says it as a joke about procedure, which is what it is, and blows on his hands, and does not notice that you have stopped.

acts.text:
"Countersign," Habrach says, and goes to a drawer, and is back in ninety seconds.

It is not a difficulty. It is not even a delay. The Administratum's Vardan reconciliation office holds a standing instrument covering the effects of Ordo officers deceased in service on this world, signed once, in advance, renewed every four years since 963, and it covers this and it covers everything.

A. KESH.

Habrach reads the name off it without any interest at all, because it is the name that is on everything, and opens the inner gate.

It takes four days to get the crates out and laid out on the floor, because you do it yourself and you do it one at a time.

Somewhere in the third of those days a query goes up from Stack Theta to a reconciliation office, on a standing instrument, as it does every time, and is not read by anybody, and is filed.

[ CAGE_OPEN ]

You lay the room out on the floor of Stack Theta.

Not the objects — the *order*. Nine positions, taken off eleven pict-captures and a stock return and a board with three pieces on the wrong squares, chalked onto concrete in a cage at four degrees, with a clerk watching you do it and saying nothing.

And then you read it backwards, because that is what the boots said, and because the boots are in your coat and were never on any list.

It is all there. Four days late, one remove from the room, reassembled out of paper and a pair of boots — but it is all there, and it holds, and the address is the address and the hour is the hour and the six days are the six days.

Habrach helps you carry the crates back at the end of it and does not ask a single question, and at the gate he says, "You'll want the manifest number for your file," and gives it to you, and it is the number of a document that says seven.

Crase hears about it inside the week. She does not raise it and she is entirely warm about it when you raise it yourself, and what she says is that she is glad you had the time.

[ ROOM_READ_FULL — CIPHER_HALF_ROOM ]

You send up for the Act I file, because the positions are in the pict-captures and the pict-captures are in the file.

It comes back in an hour, which is fast, and it is thin, which is not.

The scene captures are there — four of them, where you are fairly sure there were eleven, and the four are the four of the body. The autopsy entry is a hundred and ninety words and you would have said it was longer. Where you remember *no toxin, no coercion residue, and no psychic trace were detected* it says *no residue was detected*, which is a shorter sentence that means a different thing.

Nothing has been struck. There is no gap, no annotation, no amendment mark and no line about a revision, because a document that has been revised says so and this one has nothing to say.

You sit on a crate in the cold for a while with a file in your hands that does not agree with you about what is in it.

Then you go up and get on with the day, because there is no office in the Imperium you could take this to that would not conclude, correctly and on the evidence, that you had misremembered.

You chalk out what you have on the concrete and stand over it.

It does not close. There is a shape here and it is nearly a sentence and it is not one, and standing in the cold looking at it you understand something you would rather not have: he did not leave a message that could be partly read.

He left one that worked or did not.

What is on the floor is worth exactly as much as an eleven-week-old rumour, and you rub it out with your boot, and go back to the crates.

exits.text: Up out of Theta, four degrees warmer at every landing.

strings.no_such_thing: A cage, a floor, and nine boxes. There is nothing else down here and there never has been.
strings.already_read: You have looked twice. Habrach is cold and you are on his time.
strings.no_terminal: There is no cogitator in Theta. There is no heating in Theta.
strings.read_room_locked: Not here. The room is four tiers up and eight days gone.
